content: Bronchiolitis is the most common reason for hospital admission among infants in high-income countries. Acute viral bronchiolitis is characterized by airway obstruction and turbulent gas flow. Heliox, a mixture of helium and oxygen, has been proposed as a therapy to improve gas flow through high-resistance airways and reduce the work of breathing. This review focused on studies that evaluated the effects of adding heliox to standard medical care for infants with acute bronchiolitis. The objective of the review was to assess the impact of heliox inhalation therapy, in addition to standard care, on clinical outcomes such as the rate of endotracheal intubation, emergency department discharge rates, duration of treatment for respiratory distress, and pulmonary function as measured by clinical respiratory scores. The authors conducted a comprehensive search of multiple databases, including CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and the NIH website, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-RCTs involving heliox therapy in infants with acute bronchiolitis. Data extraction and quality assessment were performed independently by two reviewers. Seven trials involving 447 infants under two years of age with respiratory distress due to viral bronchiolitis were included. Most of the infants (378) were recruited from pediatric intensive care units (PICUs), while one trial included 69 infants from an emergency department. The age of participants varied, with some trials focusing on infants under nine months and others on those under three months. Five trials required positive tests for respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) for inclusion, while the remaining two were conducted during bronchiolitis seasons. Seven different heliox inhalation protocols were used across the studies. In the PICU setting, heliox therapy did not significantly reduce the rate of intubation, with a risk ratio (RR) of 2.73 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.96 to 7.75) based on four trials involving 408 infants. The evidence quality was low. In the emergency department, heliox therapy did not increase the rate of discharge, with an RR of 0.51 (95% CI 0.17 to 1.55) based on one trial involving 69 infants. The evidence quality was moderate. Additionally, heliox therapy did not reduce the overall duration of treatment for respiratory distress, with a mean difference (MD) of -0.19 days (95% CI -0.56 to 0.19) based on two trials involving 320 infants. The evidence quality was moderate. However, in a subgroup of infants with severe respiratory distress who were started on nasal continuous positive airway pressure (nCPAP) from the beginning, heliox therapy reduced the duration of treatment by 0.76 days (95% CI -1.45 to -0.08) in one trial involving 21 infants. The evidence quality for this finding was low. No adverse events related to heliox inhalation were reported in any of the studies. Importantly, infants treated with heliox had significantly lower mean clinical respiratory scores within the first hour of treatment compared to those treated with air or oxygen. The MD was -1.04 (95% CI -1.60 to -0.48) based on four trials involving 138 infants. The evidence quality was moderate. However, there was statistical heterogeneity in this outcome, which persisted even after excluding a study that used a standard high-concentration reservoir mask. Possible reasons for this heterogeneity include the small sample sizes of the trials and differences in baseline disease severity, as measured by the modified Wood Clinical Asthma Score (m-WCAS), which ranged from less than two to more than seven in infants treated with heliox. The authors concluded that current evidence suggests heliox therapy may significantly reduce clinical respiratory distress scores within the first hour of treatment in infants with acute RSV bronchiolitis, regardless of the specific heliox protocol used. However, heliox did not reduce the rate of intubation, emergency department discharge rates, or the overall duration of treatment for respiratory distress. Heliox may reduce the treatment duration in infants requiring CPAP for severe respiratory distress. Further research is needed to standardize heliox application protocols and include only infants with severe respiratory distress, as those with mild bronchiolitis are unlikely to benefit. Such studies would help clarify the role of heliox in the management of severe bronchiolitis.
